clue.text: Fireworks music?

parts.note: a flashy solo passage in a concerto is a display of musical fireworks, not music played at a fireworks show

explanation.definitionFit: This is the virtuoso solo passage near the end of a concerto movement where the soloist shows off.

clue.text: Undressed in unusual act-it's an intimate show

indicators.note: one piece sits inside the other, as the clue says one is in the second
unusual signals that the letters of act are put in a different order

parts.note: undressed means bare, without clothes

explanation.surface: A risqué stage act involving nudity is described as an intimate show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unusual' turns ACT into CAT, and 'in' puts BARE inside it: CA-BARE-T.
explanation.definitionFit: A nightclub entertainment in a small venue is an intimate show, close to its audience.

clue.text: Badly severed, establish claim to proper treatment

indicators.note: badly signals that the letters of severed are put in a jumbled order

explanation.surface: Someone whose limb was badly cut off makes a case for proper medical care.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Badly' rearranges SEVERED.
explanation.definitionFit: To merit something is to have a rightful claim to it, such as fitting treatment.

clue.text: Nozzle has nothing in it-it was used for the last drop

definitions.text: it was used for the last drop

indicators.note: the clue says the nozzle has nothing in it, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: nozzle is slang for the nose
nothing is zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: A hose nozzle is empty, having delivered its final drip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nozzle' is slang for the nose; 'in' puts O inside it. The definition refers to the hangman's rope and the drop through the gallows trapdoor.
explanation.definitionFit: A hangman's looped rope was the device of execution by the drop from the scaffold.

clue.text: Air T-shirt incorrectly and this could result

indicators.note: incorrectly signals that the letters of air and T-shirt are put in the wrong order

explanation.surface: Wearing a T-shirt in the open air the wrong way might bring on an ailment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'incorrectly' rearranges AIR plus TSHIRT; the definition plays on joint pain from a chill.
explanation.definitionFit: Joint inflammation is a condition that could, folk wisdom says, follow exposure to cold air.

clue.text: Vivid diagram

explanation.definitionFit: Graphic means strikingly clear (vivid) and, as a noun, a chart or illustration (diagram).

clue.text: Facing him, it's what Scottish bowler' might do in frustration

definitions.text: Facing him, it's what Scottish bowler' might do in frustration

parts.words: Facing him, it's what Scottish bowler' might do in frustration
parts.note: a Scottish bowler facing this batsman would exclaim och in frustration, where go means say

explanation.surface: A Scottish bowler grows exasperated bowling to a famously stubborn batsman.
explanation.walkthrough: Graham Gooch was an England opening batsman of the 1970s to 1990s. In colloquial English 'go' can mean 'say', and 'och' is the Scots exclamation of annoyance.
explanation.definitionFit: The batsman's surname matches what a Scot would say, so the cricketer is the one being faced.

clue.text: Pretending to be moving

explanation.definitionFit: Affecting means putting on a show (pretending) and also touching the emotions (moving).

clue.text: Sneaky, low fellow — drat the scoundrel

parts.note: drat and hang (as in hang it!) are both mild curses
a dog is a contemptible rogue

explanation.surface: Someone curses a sly, base man as a scoundrel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hang it!' is a mild oath like 'drat'; 'dog' is an old word for a rotter.
explanation.definitionFit: A sneaking, shamefaced, abject person was once called this, as in a cowed look.

clue.text: Joy at No. 10 is only for so long

parts.note: joy and cheer are both gladness
the number 10 is written as the letters I and O

explanation.surface: Happiness at the Prime Minister's residence never lasts.
explanation.walkthrough: No. 10 Downing Street is the British Prime Minister's home; here '10' is just the letters I and O.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are casual British farewells, ways of saying goodbye.

clue.text: Injunction to be a good fellow and divert

definitions.text: Injunction to be a good fellow

explanation.definitionFit: Read as two words it is an order to play fair (be a sport); as one archaic verb it means to amuse or entertain.

clue.text: Crime on the part of receiver

parts.note: on the part of means from or by, the word of
a fence is a receiver of stolen goods

explanation.surface: Receiving stolen goods is itself a criminal act.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'receiver' in crime slang is a fence, who handles stolen property.
explanation.definitionFit: An unlawful act or breach of the law is a synonym for a crime.

clue.text: Element thin on the ground?

parts.note: thin, as in thin on the ground, means scarce or rare
the ground is the earth underfoot

explanation.surface: Something scarce is described as thin on the ground.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase 'thin on the ground' is split: 'thin' is RARE and 'the ground' is EARTH, with 'on' joining them.
explanation.definitionFit: The lanthanides are a group of metallic chemical elements known by this name.

clue.text: Perry's partner playfully taken with Rosie

explanation.definitionFit: Perry (pear drink) pairs with the apple drink, and the Laurie Lee memoir title (later staged as a play) puts the same drink with Rosie.

clue.text: But it is not Harris's river

definitions.text: But it is not Harris's river

parts.words: But it is not Harris's river
parts.note: Harris names a woven cloth, but the same word is also a Border river, which Harris does not own

explanation.surface: Someone points out that a river is not owned by a man called Harris.
explanation.walkthrough: Harris Tweed is cloth woven in the Outer Hebrides; the Tweed is also the river along the Scotland–England border.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a Scottish river and the cloth from Harris, so it is a river but not Harris's.

clue.text: Lend drama characters for "Utopia"

indicators.note: characters taken as letters of lend and drama, rearranged into a new word

explanation.surface: Lending stage characters to a play called Utopia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'characters' means the letters of LEND DRAMA, shuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: An idealised imaginary place of perfection is a land of dreams.

clue.text: Wigging puts king in total chaos

indicators.note: in places the word king inside the scrambled letters
chaos signals that the letters of total are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A telling-off throws a king into complete disarray.
explanation.walkthrough: 'chaos' makes TALTO from TOTAL; 'in' puts KING inside: TAL-KING-TO. A wigging is British slang for a scolding.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are informal words for a reprimand or a scolding.

clue.text: Belgian town judge and feudal superior

parts.note: Liège is a city in eastern Belgium
a Law Lord was a senior judge in Britain

explanation.surface: A judge from Belgium is also a medieval overlord.
explanation.walkthrough: A Law Lord was a senior British judge, so 'judge' gives LORD.
explanation.definitionFit: In the feudal system the master to whom a vassal owed allegiance held this title.

clue.text: Letter-opener?

parts.note: not a paper knife but the person entitled to open the letter, the one it is sent to

explanation.definitionFit: The person named on an envelope is the one who opens it.

clue.text: An orchestra playing with careless freedom

parts.note: an orchestra is a band of musicians
a show that is playing is on

explanation.surface: An orchestra performs with uninhibited spirit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'playing' gives ON, as a show running is 'on'.
explanation.definitionFit: Wild abandon is unrestrained, carefree liberty.

clue.text: Devilish sticky game for top people

definitions.text: Devilish sticky game for top people

parts.words: Devilish sticky game for top people
parts.note: a game named from the Greek for devil, played with two sticks and a string spinning a top-shaped spool

explanation.definitionFit: The juggling toy's name comes from the word for devil, and it uses hand sticks to spin a double-cone top.

clue.text: August outing has zest

indicators.note: has means the words contain the answer, held across them

explanation.surface: A summer excursion is full of enthusiasm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has' signals the letters run inside 'auGUST Outing'.
explanation.definitionFit: Enthusiastic enjoyment, relish and zest are synonyms.

clue.text: Foot enters it to make seat safer

definitions.text: Foot enters it to make seat safer

parts.words: Foot enters it to make seat safer
parts.note: a rider puts a foot into this loop hanging from the saddle, steadying the seat on a horse

explanation.definitionFit: The metal loop beside a saddle holds the rider's foot and steadies them on horseback.

clue.text: Superintend poetry in Old English

indicators.note: in places the poetry inside the abbreviation for old English

parts.note: poetry is verse

explanation.surface: Someone supervises the study of Anglo-Saxon poems.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts VERSE inside OE.
explanation.definitionFit: To supervise or direct work is a synonym.

clue.text: In the manner of a jolly warning

parts.note: à la is French for in the manner of
a jolly is slang for a Royal Marine, abbreviated RM

explanation.surface: A cheerful alert given in a certain style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jolly' is old naval slang for a Royal Marine, RM; 'à la' means 'in the style of'.
explanation.definitionFit: An alert signal of danger is a warning.

clue.text: London way… of showing peculiar dice-shape

indicators.note: peculiar signals that the letters of dice-shape are put in an odd order

explanation.surface: A London street shows off oddly shaped dice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'peculiar' rearranges DICESHAPE. Cheapside is a historic street in the City of London.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheapside is a well-known street in the City of London, an example of a London thoroughfare.

clue.text: Being rather cautious of tea on the railway

parts.note: cha (char) is British slang for tea
RY is the abbreviation for railway

explanation.surface: Someone is wary of the tea served on trains.
explanation.walkthrough: British railway tea was notoriously poor, which gives the surface; CHA is slang for tea.
explanation.definitionFit: Being wary or reluctant is the sense of this adjective.

clue.text: Might Prince Charles shortly go to the Queen?

parts.note: Charles was then Prince of Wales, abbreviated POW
ER stands for Elizabeth Regina, the Queen

explanation.surface: A question whether the heir might soon succeed his mother.
explanation.walkthrough: When this was set Charles was Prince of Wales, shortened to POW; 'go to' joins it to ER.
explanation.definitionFit: Might as a noun is strength or force.

clue.text: Model exhibition look through the window!

explanation.definitionFit: A three-dimensional scene of models is shown, and viewers often peer at it through a glass opening.

clue.text: Where, and how, nurse progresses

parts.note: a nurse works in hospital rooms for patients and her career moves forward, the word split two ways

explanation.definitionFit: Read as one word it means forward; split in two it is where a nurse works.

clue.text: Poor Danny, wearing spectacles at twelve

indicators.note: wearing means the scrambled name has the glasses on it, so one piece goes inside
poor signals that the letters of Danny are reworked badly

parts.note: spectacles look like the letters OO

explanation.surface: Unfortunate Danny has his glasses on at midday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poor' turns DANNY into NNDAY and 'wearing' puts OO, a picture of spectacles, inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Midday is twelve o'clock.

clue.text: Early earthwork revealed by turbulent rip-tide

indicators.note: turbulent signals that the letters of rip-tide are churned into a new order

explanation.surface: A rough current exposes an ancient earthwork.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turbulent' rearranges RIPTIDE. The definition means a child's mud pie, an early (childhood) earthwork, not an archaeological one.
explanation.definitionFit: A mud pie made by small children is an earth creation of early childhood.
